output.query: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis treatment protocol immunotherapy

results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included; probable disease requires four groups (or three with a teratoma) of rapid onset plus an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: All patients had antibodies in CSF, whereas about 14% were negative in serum; CSF titers related more closely to outcome than serum titers.
results.source: Gresa-Arribas N et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:167-177

results.finding: 38% had a tumor, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumor removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

results.finding: Severe intolerance to antipsychotics (rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis) was frequent in patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis who received them.
results.source: Lejuste F et al. Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm 2016;3:e280

output.summary: Published criteria and cohort data on anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: definite diagnosis rests on CSF IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies; first-line immunotherapy and tumor removal are followed by second-line agents when there is no response.

output.query: extreme delta brush EEG pattern anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis

results.finding: Extreme delta brush, rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta with superimposed 20-30 Hz beta bursts, was found in 7 of 23 adults (30%) with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and was associated with a more prolonged illness.
Extreme delta brush counts as an abnormal EEG within the probable anti-NMDAR encephalitis criteria, alongside focal or diffuse slow or disorganized activity and epileptic activity.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

output.summary: Extreme delta brush is a recognized EEG pattern in a minority of adults with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; it supports the diagnosis but its absence excludes nothing.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1 to 2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, with hydration and without NSAIDs, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).
Arrange prompt surgical removal of the left ovarian teratoma (laparoscopic, ovary-sparing where feasible) as part of first-line treatment, with gynecology.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.

Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for central hypoventilation requiring oxygen, autonomic instability (heart rate 110-140, labile blood pressure, diaphoresis), repeated seizures and catatonia, with airway assessment and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation before cyclophosphamide.
Treat agitation, insomnia and catatonia (waxy flexibility) with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first.
Stop the combined oral contraceptive while she is immobilized in the ICU and receiving IVIG (venous thromboembolism risk) and give VTE prophylaxis.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioral management; gynecology for the teratoma.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) or other viral encephalitis
differential.key_features: CSF HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV and enterovirus PCR negative on an LP about 2 weeks after onset; MRI medial temporal and insular FLAIR signal without hemorrhage or restricted diffusion; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B or AMPA receptor)
differential.key_features: Serum neuronal-surface panel negative (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, DPPX) and onconeural antibodies negative; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

Generalized seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, central hypoventilation, autonomic instability, extreme delta brush and CSF pleocytosis with oligoclonal bands are not explained by a psychiatric disorder.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced psychosis or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
differential.key_features: No antipsychotic or new drug before the illness; urine drug screen and alcohol negative; CK only 185 U/L; rigidity and fever accompany seizures and dyskinesias.
ANA negative and no systemic features; a sister with SLE does not change this; CSF anti-GluN1 explains the syndrome.

key_clinical_evidence: Subacute onset over 2 weeks, after a febrile viral-like prodrome, of paranoia and behavioral change, disorganized speech with mutism, generalized seizures, orofacial dyskinesias and chorea, reduced responsiveness (GCS 13) and autonomic instability with central hypoventilation: all six Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titer 1:320) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive 1:80 is read with the CSF.

MRI shows bilateral medial temporal (left greater than right) and right insular FLAIR signal without restricted diffusion, hemorrhage or enhancement; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds, and the negative CSF HSV PCR excludes HSV encephalitis.
EEG shows extreme delta brush, generalized rhythmic delta and a subclinical left temporal seizure; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Pelvic ultrasound shows a 2.8 cm left ovarian mature cystic teratoma: its removal is part of first-line treatment.
Earlier immunotherapy and tumor removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A viral-like prodrome precedes about 70% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it does not establish viral encephalitis, which CSF PCR addresses.
red_herrings.data_point: Flu-like prodrome (mild fever, headache, malaise) two weeks before the neuropsychiatric syndrome.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a primary viral encephalitis (HSV) or post-viral psychosis; tempts the agent to commit to empiric antiviral therapy without pursuing autoimmune workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG and CSF inflammation accompany the behavioral change and must be explained before a psychiatric diagnosis is accepted.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (irritability, paranoia, emotional outbursts) in a previously well 31-year-old with no psychiatric history.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic-encephalopathy framing instead of the neurological work-up.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome needs antipsychotic exposure and a markedly raised CK; this mild rise reflects seizures and dyskinesias and does not change management.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises concern for neuroleptic malignant syndrome or rhabdomyolysis when combined with dyskinesias and hyperthermia.

patient.history_present_illness: A 31-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric or neurological history presents to the emergency department after being brought in by her partner for progressive behavioral changes and a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. Approximately two weeks ago, the patient developed a flu-like illness with mild fever, headache, and malaise lasting 3-4 days, which resolved spontaneously. Within days of the viral prodrome resolving, her partner noticed personality changes including irritability, mood swings, and uncharacteristic emotional outbursts at work. She became increasingly paranoid, accusing coworkers of conspiring against her, and was reported to have had a screaming episode at school that led to her being sent home. Over the following week, she developed progressive confusion, insomnia, and difficulty with short-term memory. She began having difficulty performing basic tasks such as cooking and following television programs. Her speech became disorganized with periods of mutism alternating with incomprehensible utterances. Three days prior to presentation, her partner witnessed repetitive abnormal movements including lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and involuntary hand movements. Two days ago she had her first witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds, which self-terminated. She has since had two additional witnessed seizures. Yesterday she became increasingly unresponsive, with intermittent agitation requiring physical restraint. Her partner reports episodes of profuse sweating and noted that her heart rate seemed rapid. She has had no recent travel, no known sick contacts beyond the initial viral illness, no tick bites, and no new medications. She has not consumed alcohol excessively or used recreational drugs. She had a normal gynecological examination three months ago.

neurological_exam.additional: Autonomic instability: episodic tachycardia (HR 110-140), labile blood pressure, profuse diaphoresis. Episodes of central hypoventilation requiring supplemental oxygen observed during monitoring. Waxy flexibility noted on passive limb positioning.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing inaccurate bilaterally, though limited by poor cooperation and involuntary movements. Heel-to-shin not attempted due to patient's inability to follow commands consistently.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive 3mm bilaterally. Orofacial dyskinesias present: repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and jaw movements. Intermittent left-sided facial twitching. Extraocular movements full but with saccadic intrusions. No papilledema on fundoscopy. Corneal reflexes intact. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Unsteady, wide-based gait with tendency to veer to the left. Requires two-person assist. Unable to perform tandem gait.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but disoriented to date and place. GCS 13 (E4 V4 M5). Intermittent periods of agitation alternating with flat affect. Unable to perform serial 7s. Immediate recall 2/3 objects, delayed recall 0/3 at 5 minutes. Intermittent echolalia and perseveration noted. Speech is dysarthric with occasional paraphasic errors.
neurological_exam.motor: Tone increased in all four extremities with intermittent cogwheel rigidity in upper limbs. Strength 4/5 throughout, limited by poor cooperation. Intermittent choreiform movements of both hands. Stereotypic right-hand fidgeting movements observed.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, triceps 3+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 3+ bilaterally. Patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to pain in all four extremities. Light touch and proprioception difficult to assess reliably due to altered mental status and poor cooperation.
